title: Elementary Theory of Alpha Decay
short_intro: Alpha decay is a radioactive process in which an unstable atomic nucleus ejects an alpha particle, transforming into a daughter nucleus with a mass number smaller by 4 and an atomic number smaller by 2. The elementary quantum-mechanical theory explains this process through quantum tunneling of the pre-formed alpha particle through a Coulomb potential barrier.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Definition of alpha decay, conservation laws of mass number and atomic number, Geiger-Nuttall empirical law relating decay constant and range of alpha particles, and basic energetics (Q-value).
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Quantum mechanical tunneling model (Gamow theory), barrier penetration probability, derivation of decay constant, and dependence on disintegration energy.

prerequisites: Conservation of energy and linear momentum in nuclear reactions
De Broglie wavelength and elementary wave mechanics
Coulomb's law and potential energy of point charges

concept_notes.heading: Energetics of Alpha Decay
bullets: The Q-value of alpha decay is defined as Q = (m_P - m_D - m_alpha) c², representing the total energy released during the transformation.
The disintegration energy Q is shared between the recoiling daughter nucleus and the alpha particle inversely proportional to their masses to conserve linear momentum.
For an alpha decay to occur spontaneously, the Q-value must be strictly positive (Q > 0).

concept_notes.heading: The Coulomb Potential Barrier
bullets: Outside the nuclear radius R, the potential energy experienced by the alpha particle is purely electrostatic: V(r) = (1 / 4πε_0) (2 Z e²) / r.

At the nuclear surface, the attractive nuclear forces form a potential well, while the repulsive electrostatic force forms a barrier of height V_max exceeding the kinetic energy of the alpha particle.
Classically, an alpha particle with kinetic energy less than the barrier height cannot escape the nucleus.

concept_notes.heading: Quantum Mechanical Tunneling (Gamow Theory)
bullets: According to quantum mechanics, particles possess a non-zero probability wave that penetrates classically forbidden regions.
George Gamow treated the alpha particle as an independent entity bouncing back and forth inside the nuclear potential well, striking the barrier f times per second.
The decay constant λ is the product of the assault frequency f and the quantum transmission coefficient T (λ = f T).

concept_notes.heading: Geiger-Nuttall Law
bullets: Geiger and Nuttall established an empirical linear relation between the logarithm of the decay constant (λ) and the logarithm of the range (R) of the emitted alpha particle in air: log λ = A log R + B.
Higher energy alpha particles have shorter lifetimes (larger decay constants) because they encounter a thinner and lower effective potential barrier.
The law is naturally explained by Gamow's tunneling theory.

derivations.title: Transmission Coefficient for a Coulomb Barrier
derivations.conditions: Assuming a rectangular barrier approximation or WKB approximation for the Coulomb potential V(r) = (2Ze²/(4πε_0 r))
steps: Apply the WKB approximation to find the decay constant or barrier penetration factor P = exp(-2 ∫_{R}^{r_0} k(r) dr), where k(r) = &sqrt;(2μ(V(r) - E)) / ℏ.
Evaluate the integral between the nuclear radius R and the classical turning point r_0 where V(r_0) = E.
Perform the integration analytically by substituting r = r_0 cos²θ to obtain the Gamow factor.
Express the transmission coefficient P in terms of the charge numbers, fine structure constant, and velocity of the alpha particle.
derivations.result: P = exp(-2 G), where G = ( π Z_1 Z_2 e² / 4πε_0 ℏ v ) - 4 ( Z_1 Z_2 R / 4πε_0 ℏ^2 μ )^(1/2)

derivations.title: Kinetic Energy Distribution of Decay Products
derivations.conditions: Rest frame of the parent nucleus, conservation of total energy and linear momentum.
steps: Set initial momentum of parent nucleus to zero: p_P = 0.
Apply momentum conservation: p_alpha + p_D = 0, hence p_alpha = -p_D.
Express kinetic energy in terms of momentum: K_alpha = p_alpha^2 / (2m_alpha) and K_D = p_D^2 / (2m_D).
Substitute Q = K_alpha + K_D and eliminate momentum to relate K_alpha directly to Q and masses.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Nuclear Potential Well and Coulomb Barrier
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Potential energy V(r) on y-axis versus radial distance r on x-axis, showing a deep attractive well inside nuclear radius R, a Coulomb barrier peak of height V_max, and a horizontal line representing alpha particle energy E.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Illustrates that the alpha particle energy E is less than the barrier peak V_max, making classical escape impossible, yet quantum tunneling allows escape.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Frequently asked in conceptual multiple-choice questions to explain why alpha particles emerge with energy less than the barrier height.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Geiger-Nuttall Plot
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Straight lines plotting log(λ) against log(R) for different radioactive series (Uranium, Thorium, Actinium).
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Shows parallel straight lines confirming that isotopes with higher energy (longer range R) have exponentially shorter half-lives.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Tested via interpretation of slopes and intercepts or matching decay constants with particle ranges.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Cloud Chamber Track of Alpha Particles
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Straight, dense, parallel ionization tracks of uniform length originating from a point source.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Demonstrates that monoenergetic alpha particles travel a well-defined range in matter before losing all their energy.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Used in experimental physics questions related to the detection and characteristic properties of alpha radiation.

solved_numericals.question: Calculate the Q-value of the alpha decay of 226Ra to 222Rn, given the masses: m(^226Ra) = 226.0254 u, m(^222Rn) = 222.0175 u, and m(α) = 4.0015 u. (1 u = 931.5 MeV/c^2)
solution_steps: Write the mass defect Δm = m(Parent) - m(Daughter) - m(α).
Substitute the given atomic masses: Δm = 226.0254 u - 222.0175 u - 4.0015 u.
Multiply by 931.5 MeV/u to find Q: Q = 0.0064 × 931.5 MeV.

solved_numericals.question: An alpha particle is emitted with a kinetic energy of 4.8 MeV from a nucleus with atomic number Z = 90. Assuming the daughter nucleus has mass number A = 228, find the kinetic energy of the recoiling daughter nucleus.
solution_steps: Identify the given values: K_alpha = 4.8 MeV, m_alpha ≈ 4 u, m_D ≈ A - 4 = 228 - 4 = 224 u.
Use momentum conservation relation between kinetic energies: K_D / K_alpha = m_alpha / m_D.
Substitute the mass values: K_D = 4.8 MeV × (4 / 224).
Evaluate the division: 4 / 224 = 1 / 56, so K_D = 4.8 / 56 MeV.

solved_numericals.question: If the disintegration energy Q for an alpha decay is 5.4 MeV, determine the exact kinetic energy of the emitted alpha particle, taking the exact mass of the alpha particle as 4.0015 u and the daughter nucleus mass as 218 u.
solution_steps: Recall the formula relating alpha kinetic energy to Q: K_alpha = Q [ m_D / (m_alpha + m_D) ].
Substitute the given mass values: m_D = 218 u, m_alpha = 4.0015 u, total mass = 222.0015 u.

assumptions_and_limitations: The alpha particle is assumed to pre-form inside the nucleus prior to emission, though nuclear structure models view it as a cluster formation probability.
The WKB approximation used in calculating the barrier penetration assumes the potential varies slowly compared to the de Broglie wavelength of the alpha particle.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Alpha particles possess kinetic energy greater than the height of the Coulomb barrier inside the nucleus.
common_misconceptions.correct: The kinetic energy of the alpha particle is less than the barrier peak, and it escapes via quantum mechanical tunneling.
common_misconceptions.why: Classically, an energy deficit would prevent escape; quantum mechanics permits barrier penetration.

common_misconceptions.wrong: All alpha particles emitted from a specific radioactive isotope have continuous kinetic energy spectra like beta decay.
common_misconceptions.correct: Alpha particles from a given transition are monoenergetic.
common_misconceptions.why: Two-body decay kinematics dictates a fixed energy sharing between the alpha particle and the daughter nucleus.

quick_revision: Alpha decay reduces mass number by 4 and atomic number by 2.
Spontaneous alpha decay requires a positive Q-value.
Gamow theory successfully explains alpha decay via quantum tunneling through the Coulomb barrier.
Geiger-Nuttall law states a linear relation between log(λ) and log(R).
